lines: In 1957, a French film director invented a board game about conquering the world.
His name was Albert Lamorisse. The same year, his short film The Red Balloon won an Oscar.
Two years later, Parker Brothers brought his game to America, and called it Risk.
And for sixty years, players have repeated the same piece of advice.
The defender has the advantage.
Ties go to the defense. So never attack unless you clearly outnumber them.
So we built Risk in code, with the official dice rules.
And we fought every battle ten thousand times.
Every roll.
Every casualty.
Then we checked every result against the exact math.
And the old advice is wrong. Not a little wrong.
By the end of this video, you'll know when a smaller army beats a bigger one,
the one attack you should almost never make,
and exactly how many armies you need to take any territory.
Part one. One roll.
Here's how a fight works.
The attacker rolls up to three red dice. The defender rolls up to two.
You line them up, highest against highest, second against second.
Whoever rolls higher wins that pair. And if it's a tie, the defender wins.
So the defender wins every tie. That's where the legend comes from.
But the attacker has something better. A third die.
With three dice, the attacker gets to throw away the lowest one.
So their two best dice are usually higher than the defender's two.
We rolled three against two, ten thousand times.
The attacker won both pairs 37 percent of the time.
The defender won both only 29 percent.
And they split one each 34 percent.
On average, every roll costs the attacker 0.92 armies, and the defender 1.08.
In a full-size fight, the attacker is the one with the edge.
But that edge disappears the moment the attacker runs low.
Attack with two dice into two, and the math flips.
Now the defender wins both pairs 45 percent of the time.
And one die into two is the worst move in the game.
You lose that roll 75 percent of the time.
So the rule isn't that defense is strong. It's that small attacks are weak.
Part two. The whole battle.
One roll is just a moment. Real battles go on until somebody runs out.
So we simulated complete battles. Every attack keeps rolling until the defender is wiped out, or the attacker is down to the one army that has to stay home.
Start small. Two armies attacking one defender.
Only one of them can fight, so it's one die against one.
The attacker wins 42 percent of the time. Worse than a coin flip.
Three against two?
Just 36 percent.
Five against five?
36 percent. So far, the legend looks right.
But watch what happens as the armies get bigger.
Ten against ten, 48 percent.
Twenty against twenty, 58.
Thirty against thirty, 63.
The bigger the battle, the more the attacker wins.
And here's the part nobody believes.
Twenty armies in your territory. Twenty defenders on the other side.
One of yours has to stay behind. So you're really attacking with nineteen against twenty.
And you still win 58 percent of the time.
A smaller army, beating a bigger one, more often than not.
Why? Because in a long battle, the attacker keeps rolling three dice almost the whole time.
And every one of those rolls tilts toward the attacker.
The defender's tie advantage only matters at the very end, when the attacker is down to one or two dice.
Part three. How many armies you really need.
So let's answer the question every player asks before they attack.
How many armies do I need to be safe?
We'll call safe a four in five chance of taking the territory.
One defender? You need 4 armies in your territory.
Two defenders? 6.
Three defenders? 7.
Five defenders? 9.
Ten defenders? 15.
And twenty defenders? 25.
Look at the pattern.
Against small stacks, you need two or three times their number. Against big stacks, you only need about a quarter more.
That's why the worst attacks in Risk are the little ones.
Two armies poking at one. Three poking at two.
They feel cheap. But they burn armies and usually fail.
A real attack is big, and it goes all the way.
Twenty five against twenty? You take it 82 percent of the time.
Part four. What this means for the whole game.
If big attacks win, then splitting your armies across the map is the real mistake.
One stack of twenty beats four stacks of five.
Because each stack of five is in the zone where the attacker barely wins half the time.
And it explains why the classic advice to grab Australia works.
Australia has only one way in. So you can pile every army on one border.
You become the giant stack. And giant stacks win.
South America works the same way, with two ways in.
Asia pays the biggest bonus, seven armies a turn. But it has five borders to hold.
Five borders means five thin stacks. And thin stacks are exactly what a big attack eats.
So is the defender's advantage real?
Only in small fights. In big battles, the attacker wins, even outnumbered.
Nineteen against twenty, and the attacker still wins 58 percent of the time.
Don't poke. Stack up. And when you go, go big.
